title: Elastic Cloud Pricing: Costs by Tier (2026 Guide)
summary: Elastic Cloud pricing charges hourly by resource consumption, not per seat. Your actual bill depends on deployment size and usage beyond the entry price.
body_markdown:
## Watching Elastic Cloud spend with Activepieces


Activepieces won't make Elastic Cloud cheaper. It can tell you the bill is drifting before the invoice does, and because every plan, free included, has unlimited flows, you can run one check per deployment without hitting a flow cap.


That is the part of self-hosting's hidden labor you can automate.


Cost per run applies here too. The Activepieces pricing page lists 1 credit per flow run, any number of steps, so a four-step check that fires once a day uses about 30 of the free plan's 1,000 monthly credits.


Zapier's per-task billing and Make's per-module billing, as set out on their own pricing pages, would each count the four steps separately, so you're charged four times per execution. A surprise at month end costs a full cycle of overspend.


### What the Elastic Cloud spend workflow does


It is a scheduled flow with four steps. A timer trigger starts it on a cadence you choose. An HTTP step then calls Elastic's APIs to pull current usage for your deployment.


Usage then goes to a condition step that compares it against a budget you define. If the threshold is crossed, a final step posts to a channel, such as a Slack room or an email list, so a person sees it.


The canvas reads top to bottom: a trigger, a condition that routes the path, and notification steps below it. That last step can be any of the 747 integrations, so the alert lands wherever your on-call already looks.


Swap the lead-qualification steps for usage, budget and alert, and you have the same skeleton. The point to take from it is that the logic is visible, so whoever inherits the flow can see why an alert fired without reading code.


Treat what this adds as monitoring only. It reads numbers and reports them. Tier, region, storage and data transfer still set what you pay, and changing those remains your decision.


You also take on a small maintenance job: if the API response changes, your flow breaks quietly unless you test it.


### When Elastic Cloud built-in alerts are enough


If your question is simply 'tell me when spend crosses a line,' start with the alerting and billing notifications Elastic already provides in its console.


They cost you no build time and no flow to maintain, and for a single deployment with a steady workload they're usually sufficient.


Reach for a custom workflow when the rule is yours rather than the vendor's. A budget per team, a comparison across several deployments, or a message routed into the channel where your on-call already looks all qualify.


Without one of those needs, the extra moving part is a cost, not a saving.
